/data/api_link	https://api.artic.edu/api/v1/artworks/12634
/data/title	Wine Container
/data/date_display	Western Zhou dynasty ( 1046–771 BC ), late 11th century BC
/data/description	The bulging, curvilinear silhouette of this house-shaped wine container is emphasized by prominent, hooked flanges, which also accent the surface divisions created by sectional mold casting. The elements of surface decoration—high relief monster (taotie) masks, crested and plumed birds, and dragons with reverted heads are extravagantly shaped: Fringes with elaborate hooks and quills, their curves and coils extend and replicate to symmetrically fill the divided panels of the body and lid. Identical dedicatory inscriptions cast within the interior of the base and lid read: "Rong zi [Son of Rong] made [this] precious sacrificial vessel." Such inscriptions, studied as historical documents as well as calligraphic art, contribute to our understanding of the chronology and patronage of ancient Chinese bronzes.
/data/medium_display	Bronze
/data/inscriptions	Identical inscriptions cast inside basin and lid: Rong Zi made this precious vessel
/data/provenance_text	Ching Tsai Loo (1880‒1957), Paris and New York; sold to Kate Sturges Buckingham (1858–1937), Chicago [Kate served as executor of her sister Lucy Maud Buckingham's estate and continued expanding Lucy's collection following her death in 1920]; given to the Art Institute of Chicago, 1932.
/data/department_title	Arts of Asia
